lesson.title: Assembly Line in the Cytoplasm: How Polysomes Multiply Output
lesson.summary: A polysome forms when several ribosomes translate the same mRNA molecule at the same time, each one at its own position along the transcript, allowing a cell to produce many copies of a protein from a single message at once.
lesson.body:
Translation of a single mRNA does not usually involve just one ribosome working alone from start to finish. As soon as the first ribosome clears the region around the start codon and moves into elongation, that stretch of mRNA becomes available again, and a second small ribosomal subunit can begin its own round of initiation behind it, followed by a third, and often more. Each ribosome then moves independently along the same mRNA, 5' to 3', synthesizing its own copy of the encoded protein at its own stage of elongation. Viewed under an electron microscope, this produces a striking image: several ribosomes spaced out along a single strand of mRNA, resembling beads strung along a thread. This whole assembly, one mRNA with multiple ribosomes translating it simultaneously, is called a polysome, or polyribosome.

The advantage this arrangement gives a cell is straightforward. In roughly the time it would take a single ribosome to translate a message once, a polysome allows several ribosomes to each produce a full copy of the same protein, multiplying output from one mRNA molecule many times over without requiring the cell to transcribe additional copies of the gene. For proteins in high demand, or for mRNAs that are relatively short-lived, this is a substantial efficiency gain.

Where and when polysomes form differs between prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and the difference traces back to something covered earlier in this unit: the presence of a nuclear envelope. Bacteria have no nucleus, so translation can begin on an mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing it, with ribosomes queuing up behind the polymerase itself and coupling transcription directly to translation. In a eukaryotic cell, the nuclear envelope keeps those processes separated. Capping, splicing, and polyadenylation, the modifications covered earlier in this unit, all have to be completed and the finished mRNA exported to the cytoplasm before any ribosome can load onto it, so a eukaryotic polysome always forms on a fully processed, mature transcript rather than a growing one. Either way, the underlying picture is the same: a polysome is simply ordinary translation, built from the same ribosomes, tRNAs, codons, and start and stop signals described throughout this unit, happening many times over on one message at once.
